review_text_raw:
[h1] Hacknet [/h1]
[b] An interface so real, you probably shouldn't play it in public [/b]

[h1] Run-through [/h1]

Hacknet is a storytelling, hacking simulation game developed by Team Fractal Alligator and Published by Fellow Traveller. Featuring programming puzzles, intense challenges, and an amazing soundtrack, it's time to dive into the deepest corners of the web.

With the death of the hacker "Bit", you're suddenly dragged in the underground world of the hacking community. Contacted by his failsafe system, Bit sends you very specific instructions so that Hacknet-OS, the security system he created, won't fall in the wrong hands. Acting as the spiritual successor to Uplink, Hacknet adds story and spice to mere actions and command lines.

[h1] Pros: [/h1]

• Amazing story
• Simplistic and easy to navigate UI. You can do everything the game asks you to without ever having to switch tabs up
• Challenging and entertaining puzzles
• The music feels always on point with the situation
• Mod support
• Tons of fun little Easter Eggs

[h1] Cons: [/h1]

• The tutorial is by all means too short and the game's content too wide. Might feel daunting for some players approaching the genre
• As most hacking games, don't expect accurate hacking sequences

[h1] Gameplay: in depth [/h1]

[u][b] General information [/b][/u]
Hacknet is one of those games that tend to surprise you in the best way possible. It's a game that I approached really carefully and ended up playing for hours on. The mystery around Bit's death is the most important part of the story, indeed, but Hacknet does an amazing job in giving us a handful of side missions and side stories to enrich our experience with. In our pursuit of the truth, in fact, we will stumble upon many different factions of Hackers, each of them acting accordingly to their own creeds - for example, there's a faction that wishes for people to perceive hackers as "decent" people rather than being demonised, a faction that just acts on whims and another that takes only the best hackers under its protective wing and offers them a proper job.

Even though Hacknet presents itself as a hacking game, it's quite obvious that we can't expect it to be 100% accurate on how it tackles the thematic: hacking servers and personal computers is actually really easy and requires the use of just about four or five command lines. It's clear that Hacknet's puzzle aspect comes from being able to understand what the missions are asking us to do at every given time, other than being able to enter said servers. Hacknet is a game that requires the player to be attentive and read carefully through every folder once we've hacked a device. Useful information hides everywhere.

There's a huge spectrum of missions to pick from: tinkering with websites strings, entering someone's personal mobile device, adding a degree to a student from their university's site, putting someone's names in the deceased list records and so on so forth.

Even though the game feels very linear, it is far from that. There are a lot of hidden riddles that will present you with extra hacking challenges and reward you with useful .exe files upon completing them. Successfully entering the CSEC also awards you with the ThemeChanger.exe, whereas you felt like customizing your x-system.exe program.

The soundtrack is perhaps the most enjoyable part of the whole game, by far. It's amazing how it always fits perfectly. It's relaxing if you're just skimming through the available servers, it picks up if you're hacking and you're about to get traced, it's got funny tunes if you stumble upon mini-games.

Overall, a nice experience with engaging content and features. Will rarely ever feeling boring as you're driven on by the need to know what truly happened and, of course, to become the best hacker out there.

[u][b] Content [/b][/u]
Hacknet offers a good spectrum of activities throughout the game. However, even with many different options to pick from, eventually, it will fall in a loop of things "we've already seen over and over". About ~10 to ~30 hours of gameplay.

[h1] Technical Analysis [/h1]

[u][b] Graphics [/b][/u]
A 2D interface with very basic graphics and art style. We are given the opportunity to change between a few themes throughout the game but besides that not much else.
Even so, the simplicity of it all is what makes Hacknet especially pleasing to the eye and also helps with not feeling too drained by reading walls of text.

[u][b] Music [/b][/u]
For such a small game, Hacknet surprises with a spectacular range of OSTs for many different situations and specific missions both. It's amazing how intense it gets in the right bits, making the player sweat as they try to complete their missions.

[u][b] HUD [/b][/u]
The HUD presents different sections. In the center, we have the main interface, through here we will visualize all the information on websites and in their files and logs. To its left and right there are two more columns, one used to keep track of what we're doing through notes or to see if we're almost done using a certain command, and the other used as the console where all the magic will happen. Depending on which theme we're using, these two boxes are interchangeable.
To the bottom, there is a fourth box: in here we will keep track of all the servers, networks and devices we've unlocked through our hacking deeds. Thanks to this we are able to hop back to them anytime we might need to do so, even though it rarely happens in this game. After having played for a few hours, however, and having unlocked a handful of servers, I must say that the map has started to feel very cluttered, with servers' buttons almost overlapping each other.

[u][b] Bugs Encountered [/b][/u]
None. Smooth and bugs free experience. Over the years the team really ironed them all out. A job well done.

[h1] Wrapping up [/h1]

Hacknet is one of the best deals out there for its genre. Hours on end of programming and hacking activities either as a villain or as a vigilante of the deep web are absolutely worth the price the game asks for.


[h1] RATING: 8.5/10 [/h1]

review_text_raw:
[url=https://kinglink-reviews.com/2018/05/21/hacknet-review/] Full Review [/url] --  [url=http://store.steampowered.com/curator/31803828-Kinglink-Reviews/] Curator Site [/url]

Hacking games are weird. There are games with hacking as an ability such as Deus Ex or Watch Dogs but that’s not what I’m talking about. Those game have a “hacking mechanic” which at best is a mini-game and at worst is a button press. There are also games where the focus is on “hacking” systems and while it’s almost never realistic it usually can take steps in that direction and still be fun. Hacknet is one of those games, and it is an excellent example of why I enjoy those games.

So there are two sets of games I play. Normal games, stuff like Far Cry, Destiny, Bayonetta that average gamers can enjoy the same as me. Then there are the special games. I call them “programmer games” And they’re not all the same, they don’t have the same style of gameplay but most are made for the analytical mind of a programmer. Programmer games to me are games like Factorio, and pretty much every Zachtronics game (Which I will start reviewing soon, I promise, Zach your day will come!). And Uplink. Yes, Uplink is certainly there.

Uplink might be the first game I ever played where I felt a bond with the developer. I didn’t just like Uplink. I loved every minute of it. I was a novice with computers (and in some ways maybe I still am) but Uplink gave me the feeling that I was hacking into computers, and racing to beat a trace to avoid detection. Uplink was a blast. It was a great game. Hell in the back of my mind whenever I’m running a route trace (tracert) or pinging a server, I still imagine the map of the world and believe it’s following a single line on it.

I’m not the only person who liked Uplink. I can say that with absolute certainty because Hacknet clearly was developed to be similar to Uplink. Now two people can come up with the same idea, but Hacknet came out a decade after Uplink and even has a mission about someone copying “Introversion’s” game idea in Hacknet. Introversion is the name of the company that made Uplink.

Because of that, I’m sure the question comes up if this is a clone. While I have a very long version of why it doesn’t matter, the question would carry more weight if Hacknet didn’t differentiate itself from Uplink, or if Uplink was still developed. Introversion has gone on to make other amazing games, including the current “Prison Architect”. While Uplink is a clear inspiration, it’s also just the starting point, and Hacknet ran with it in so many directions that I’m impressed.

But there is one thought that Hacknet didn’t improve on Uplink. Uplink has a rather solid story, and it’s exciting from the first moment to the end of the game. I remember playing it a number of times, and the story drove me on to finish it in more than one way.

Hacknet, on the other hand, has a weaker story. Most of the story is done through missions and while there are some choices the player can make, or choose between a number of groups, there’s not really a reason or a purpose for it.

The real story of Hacknet only appears at the end and it only becomes a major event for a number of missions in a row, but it’s never has a strong pull to finish it, instead you just want to keep completing missions and because of that the story pulls you along. I feel like a lot of the story comes out of nowhere.

That’s not to say there are no interesting stories in Hacknet, but they’re more about the current mission you are on or just side stories that develop the world. It’s a shame because it’s one of the big flaws in the game in my opinion. The game feels like it tries to be open to the player making choices so it’s free-form but then backloads all the major story events to the end. I’d have loved to see the major story develop into emergency situations you deal with throughout the game and you could get the feeling you are competing against something even if you weren’t.

The bigger problem to me though is the story doesn’t tend to listen to the rules it has set up for its universe. You start the game and eventually join a hacking group. The first group are “White Hats” which means constructive hacking. They don’t exactly follow those rules, but while they can be destructive, they have a moral code that’s critical for them. It’s a good mantra to follow, and I like the idea of it.

The problem is the game never follows it up. In fact, a few missions are hollow when you realize there’s no positives or negatives for how you do jobs. The group might claim they’re “White Hats” and they told me to only delete what was necessary on one assignment. I trashed the computer and destroyed everything I could. The group never brought up my destructive nature. In fact, from that point onward, I found I could go against almost all the rules that the story developed for me.

For instance, Hacknet stresses deleting logs are important, and this was critical in Uplink. If you left logs in Uplink, people would be able to backtrace you even after you disconnected. However, in Hacknet there are two problems. First disconnecting from a server leaves a final log entry that’s deadly. In real life, you could wipe the log, have a program delete them after a timed execution or crash a server to avoid writing a disconnect if it matters. But none of these are required because of the second issue. Leaving the logs alone makes no difference. It’s a story element that doesn’t actually have gameplay attached to it.

I want to say both of these are acceptable and they are, but in fact, they annoy me a lot. The logs were a core system in Uplink and while the new game doesn’t have to be exactly like Uplink, Hacknet talks about deleting logs as critical. If they make it a major part of the story, they should require it since they said it was important.

So this has started to evolve into a discussion on the gameplay, and the gameplay is either the best part or the worst part of Hacknet. It will pretty much come down to the question of if the player can use a terminal effectively.

If you take a random server in Hacknet, you’ll usually be presented with a login prompt and the ability to “probe the network”. Almost always you will have to probe the network, from there the game will tell you what type of security measures the servers have. It might be a proxy server that you have to overload with other servers or a Firewall that means there’s an analysis program you have to run and figure out a passcode by reading off the letters that remain after analysis. You’ll almost always have to open ports on the system so you can crack the password, and you open ports by running exploits. Almost all of this is only done through the console. You can probe with the mouse, but the exploits require running the programs manually and giving them the ports.

The thing is, this is rather fun to me. I love the hacking aspects, and eventually when there’s a time limit it gets even better, trying to get everything done against a ticking clock because you have to run all the exploits, overload the proxy, figure out the firewall, and then do whatever you intended on the computer before it locks you out again.

The downside is the trace is always the same length of time. In Uplink there’s an idea of proxies which worked, as you could build a longer trace time but here, you just directly attack the computer and either have enough time, disconnect before you’re finished or run out of time.

If you want to read more and see a final score, you can see the full review with pictures at https://kinglink-reviews.com/2018/05/21/hacknet-review/  You can also check out my Curator page at If you want to hear more from me, you can show me that by following my curator at http://store.steampowered.com/curator/31803828-Kinglink-Reviews/

The bigger problem to me though is the story doesn’t tend to listen to the rules it has set up for its universe. You start the game and eventually join a hacking group. The first group are “White Hats” which means constructive hacking. They don’t exactly follow those rules, but while they can be destructive, they have a moral code that’s critical for them. It’s a good mantra to follow, and I like the idea of it. The problem is the game never follows it up. In fact, a few missions are hollow when you realize there’s no positives or negatives for how you do jobs. The group might claim they’re “White Hats” and they told me to only delete what was necessary on one assignment. I trashed the computer and destroyed everything I could. The group never brought up my destructive nature. In fact, from that point onward, I found I could go against almost all the rules that the story developed for me. For instance, Hacknet stresses deleting logs are important, and this was critical in Uplink. If you left logs in Uplink, people would be able to backtrace you even after you disconnected. However, in Hacknet there are two problems. First disconnecting from a server leaves a final log entry that’s deadly. In real life, you could wipe the log, have a program delete them after a timed execution or crash a server to avoid writing a disconnect if it matters. But none of these are required because of the second issue. Leaving the logs alone makes no difference. It’s a story element that doesn’t actually have gameplay attached to it. I want to say both of these are acceptable and they are, but in fact, they annoy me a lot. The logs were a core system in Uplink and while the new game doesn’t have to be exactly like Uplink, Hacknet talks about deleting logs as critical. If they make it a major part of the story, they should require it since they said it was important. So this has started to evolve into a discussion on the gameplay, and the gameplay is either the best part or the worst part of Hacknet. It will pretty much come down to the question of if the player can use a terminal effectively. If you take a random server in Hacknet, you’ll usually be presented with a login prompt and the ability to “probe the network”. Almost always you will have to probe the network, from there the game will tell you what type of security measures the servers have. It might be a proxy server that you have to overload with other servers or a Firewall that means there’s an analysis program you have to run and figure out a passcode by reading off the letters that remain after analysis. You’ll almost always have to open ports on the system so you can crack the password, and you open ports by running exploits. Almost all of this is only done through the console. You can probe with the mouse, but the exploits require running the programs manually and giving them the ports. The thing is, this is rather fun to me. I love the hacking aspects, and eventually when there’s a time limit it gets even better, trying to get everything done against a ticking clock because you have to run all the exploits, overload the proxy, figure out the firewall, and then do whatever you intended on the computer before it locks you out again. The downside is the trace is always the same length of time. In Uplink there’s an idea of proxies which worked, as you could build a longer trace time but here, you just directly attack the computer and either have enough time, disconnect before you’re finished or run out of time. [b]DISCLAIMER: I was provided a press review copy for the purposes of documenting the game for PCGamingWiki, a publicly-editable technical wiki for games.[/b]

What would happen if you gamified the idea that you found a copy of an OS which was so dead-simple to use, anyone with basic computer and investigative skills could hack into [i]anything[/i]? You'd get Hacknet, an excellent hacking game designed to be the spiritual successor to Uplink. Slick graphics, a sliding difficulty designed to get you introduced to the game's mechancis one-by-one, and an in-the-background story which is surprisingly pointient and explores not only how insecure computers really are to a dedicated hacker, but the ramifications, both practical and mornal, of an OS designed to hack anything.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] It's a short, satisfying hacking game which, despite how complicated it seems at the outset, eases you into its mechanics, world, and story, and gives you the surprising, satisfying feeling of being both a master hacker and Sherlock Holmes at the same time.

[h1]Is this Uplink 2.0?[/h1]
For the mandatory "Is this Uplink 2.0" part of the review: no. This is [i]not[/i] the spiritual successor hardcore fans of Uplink have been looking for because:
[list]
[*] You use a 'real' computer with fixed specs, with HacknetOS running on top of it as a VM (Virtual Machine).
[*] The game is command-line based with some GUI helpers, such as an IP map, optional GUI-based system navigation, and a note app.
[*] You can only run computer-compromising apps via command-line.
[*] The game's story, despite being subtle, in the background, and without limitations (i.e. x number of connections before game over), drives the game, and your actions are ultimately in service of the story.
[/list]

If none of the above scared you off, then read on because this spiritual sequel is, in spite of the above, a worthy one IMO...
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As mentioned above, Hacknet uses its command-line for much of the hacking, with a few GUI helpers for those tasks too cumbersome to exclusively do in the GUI, like keeping track of all the known IPs and keeping notes. Despite this, there are only a few core commands, and are remarkably easy-to-remember with repeated use - and the game is [i]very[/i] careful to ensure you do - and often relate to what they do. For example, to crack an in-game computer's SSH port, run SSHcrack [insert port number here]. This is further helped by the addition of command auto-completion - something the game teaches you how to use very quickly. So, that SSHcrack command I just mentioned? All you really need to type in is SSH, press the TAB key, add the port number, and press the Enter key. Believe me - it makes your life a [i]lot[/i] easier.

The hacking itself is simple: connect to the target, probe the computer for weaknesses, then execute programs to exploit their weaknesses. Some computers require some preperatory work, such as computers with proxies effectively require you to use other computers you've compromised to attack them, while others might require you to find a piece of cracking software to open them up, bypass a firewall by running special software to solve its encryption, and so on. At first, it isn't so difficult - just run the apps, and watch the magic happen. Later on, you'll begin to regularly encounter computers which will attempt to passively hunt your computer down and force it to reboot - complete with a giant timer showing you the exact time to failure - requiring you to run multiple apps at once. Since your computer only has so much memory, you'll need to play Tetris with the apps, shutting down those you don't need and running the ones which bypass the easiest weaknessess. Beating the clock and compromising a computer with a second to spare is an accomplishment in an of itself which never gets old.

Another good thing is the game understands how counter-intuitive command-line use is for the average user, so through the use of an initial tutorial (which can be skipped once you know how to terminate it) and missions which slowly slide up in difficulty as they teach the basic mechanics, you'll eventually come to grips with the commands you need to hack. And once you do, it starts giving you missions which, combined with the clear, clever visuals (more on those later), allow you to feel like a master hacker in a way different from other hacking games because you'll often need to do something which most hacking games leave out entirely or towards the very end.

[b]You get to be Sherlock Holmes.[/b]

You see, because people, even those with good security sense, tend to forget or excuse security issues, they also tend to leave stuff on their computers, mobile devices, and e-mail accounts. IP addresses to secret files, administrator (admin) passwords for top-secret servers and their most private e-mails - you name it, they'll leave it. As such, any good hacker needs to dig through files to find all those details so they can find what they need with the least amount of effort - allowing you to find hidden servers, open files which would otherwise be closed to you, and skip dangerous, time-consuming, and sometimes impossible system hacks by simply logging in as the administrator. You'll be surprised how satisfied you'll feel following a trail of clues to your ultimate objective, making an impossible task suddenly seem trivial - and end up finding some hilarious stuff in the process as you dig through all the files which don't matter.

All that said, there are some things which make the game easier than it should be. A key part of the gameplay is erasing anything in the system's logs indicating you were there so the authorities can't track your hacks back to you. In theory, this means deleting every log file before leaving the server; in practice, all you have to do in most cases is start deleting all the log files, disconnect from the server, wait for all the files to be deleted, then come back. "How can I delete files from a computer I just disconnected from?" you ask. You shouldn't, but the game lets you. This means that as long as the computer doesn't have a rotating admin password - and most don't - what should be down-to-the-wire hacks end up being trivial. Furthermore, any future accessing of the computer will be ignored - even if you never delete the logs after the first time.

Oddly enough, that one problem with the gameplay is...actually a bonus in my eyes, since it enables you to focus more on solving the challenging Sherlock Holmes-esque puzzles.
[h1]Story[/h1]
I can't really touch on the story much as to do so would ruin the surprise and horror it provides late in the game. I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean [i]everything[/i] - is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with.
[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. There are also some optional, subtle effects which emulate a CRT computer monitor, adding to the realism. The standout graphics come from the apps, as they show you in fun and clever ways how they're progressing, whether it shows you punching through an SSH table with every section hacked turned green or beat out an SMTP mail server's sorting algorithm to force it to shut down and open up to you.
[h1]Additional Thoughts[/h1]
I really wish the game opened up towards the middle - it would've been fun exploring the world wide web, finding hidden sub-plots as you tear through the world's computers like tissue paper, as a reprieve from the short story. Speaking of the story, I also wish it were longer - the game's puzzles were clever and unique, and I so desperately wanted more content.

Later on, you'll begin to regularly encounter computers which will attempt to passively hunt your computer down and force it to reboot - complete with a giant timer showing you the exact time to failure - requiring you to run multiple apps at once. Since your computer only has so much memory, you'll need to play Tetris with the apps, shutting down those you don't need and running the ones which bypass the easiest weaknessess. Beating the clock and compromising a computer with a second to spare is an accomplishment in an of itself which never gets old. Another good thing is the game understands how counter-intuitive command-line use is for the average user, so through the use of an initial tutorial (which can be skipped once you know how to terminate it) and missions which slowly slide up in difficulty as they teach the basic mechanics, you'll eventually come to grips with the commands you need to hack. And once you do, it starts giving you missions which, combined with the clear, clever visuals (more on those later), allow you to feel like a master hacker in a way different from other hacking games because you'll often need to do something which most hacking games leave out entirely or towards the very end. [b]You get to be Sherlock Holmes.[/b] You see, because people, even those with good security sense, tend to forget or excuse security issues, they also tend to leave stuff on their computers, mobile devices, and e-mail accounts. IP addresses to secret files, administrator (admin) passwords for top-secret servers and their most private e-mails - you name it, they'll leave it. As such, any good hacker needs to dig through files to find all those details so they can find what they need with the least amount of effort - allowing you to find hidden servers, open files which would otherwise be closed to you, and skip dangerous, time-consuming, and sometimes impossible system hacks by simply logging in as the administrator. You'll be surprised how satisfied you'll feel following a trail of clues to your ultimate objective, making an impossible task suddenly seem trivial - and end up finding some hilarious stuff in the process as you dig through all the files which don't matter. All that said, there are some things which make the game easier than it should be. A key part of the gameplay is erasing anything in the system's logs indicating you were there so the authorities can't track your hacks back to you. In theory, this means deleting every log file before leaving the server; in practice, all you have to do in most cases is start deleting all the log files, disconnect from the server, wait for all the files to be deleted, then come back. "How can I delete files from a computer I just disconnected from?" you ask. You shouldn't, but the game lets you. This means that as long as the computer doesn't have a rotating admin password - and most don't - what should be down-to-the-wire hacks end up being trivial. Furthermore, any future accessing of the computer will be ignored - even if you never delete the logs after the first time. Oddly enough, that one problem with the gameplay is...actually a bonus in my eyes, since it enables you to focus more on solving the challenging Sherlock Holmes-esque puzzles. [h1]Story[/h1] I can't really touch on the story much as to do so would ruin the surprise and horror it provides late in the game. I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean [i]everything[/i] - is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with. [h1]Graphics[/h1] The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. There are also some optional, subtle effects which emulate a CRT computer monitor, adding to the realism. The standout graphics come from the apps, as they show you in fun and clever ways how they're progressing, whether it shows you punching through an SSH table with every section hacked turned green or beat out an SMTP mail server's sorting algorithm to force it to shut down and open up to you. [h1]Additional Thoughts[/h1] I really wish the game opened up towards the middle - it would've been fun exploring the world wide web, finding hidden sub-plots as you tear through the world's computers like tissue paper, as a reprieve from the short story. Speaking of the story, I also wish it were longer - the game's puzzles were clever and unique, and I so desperately wanted more content.

review_text_raw:
[h1][i][b][u]Hacknet - 8/10[/u][/b][/i][/h1]

[u]Story[/u]
Hacknet is a puzzle game that focuses mainly on, well, hacking! At the very start of the game, you get a message from a person called "Bit", requesting a bit of hacking. [spoiler]He then, in a way, requests you to investigate his death.[/spoiler] There are also a bunch of "side" missions if you can call them that, to get good with a few other groups. I'm not saying anything else, go play it and experience it for yourself. The story is amazing and has a weird type of ending. Satisfying, though.
[spoiler]By the way, if you already know computer commands or you know how to hack, then you can skip the tutorial by writing "ps" once you get hold of the console and then "kill [i][Number shown beside "Tutorial"]"[/i][/spoiler]
[spoiler]You don't have to clear logs unless it tells you to do so in the mission briefing.[/spoiler]

[u]Storyline Length[/u]
This all depends on how good you are at puzzles, what knowledge you have of computer commands, and how fast you type. If you're great at all three of things, like me, then it should take you about an hour or two. There are quite a few tricky parts, so it might take you longer. If you're an achievement hunter, this will require at least two playthroughs to unlock all the achievements.

[u]AI[/u]
I'm not too sure if this counts as AI, but if you start to hack a really secure place, there's a chance you'll start to get traced. You have ninety seconds to finish up (and for some reason those 'ninety seconds' always go at a different speed) or else you have another minute or so to change your IP. Also, you can reply to emails and kill a guy or two but they don't really count as AI. Not in this game, anyway.

[u]Experience[/u]
This game will make you feel like a true hacker. Opening the ports of a secure server has never been easier with the programmes and knowledge you have! Firewalls? Not a problem! Proxy? Easy. 5 ports to open? Kindergarten stuff. This game, from start to finish, is a wild ride.  It'll make you laugh, make you make a hard decision even though you kinda have to do it one way, make you feel like everyone else is a peasant and you're the superior. You know, just like winning a round of CS:GO competitive against nine year olds. You can't have too many stuff open at once, which makes this game really challenging sometimes. Especially when you have to change your IP and you're extremely stressed. I'm not sure if you can move them around, I haven't tried, but the area where you decide where to connect to gets [i]extremely[/i] cluttered after a while. Would be great if you can delete some circles you're absolutely sure you won't connect to again.
Anyway, this thing actually runs on cmd which makes you feel even more of a hacker.
[spoiler]If you write "OpenCDTray" then it will open your actual computer's CD tray if you have one. Pretty damn cool![/spoiler]

[u]Graphics[/u]
Well, it's a computer desktop. Not much else to say. Deep into the game, you can get a theme changer, which changes your desktop in-game. That's about it, really.

[u]Sound[/u]
The soundtrack is not bad at all. It fits the game and can actually be quite relaxing! Although, you'll probably hear your keyboard half the time. Good stuff!

[u]Overall[/u]
I'd recommend this game to pretty much anyone. Especially those who love puzzle games, like me. This has a great story, challenging puzzles at times, and a great end. The achievements aren't too hard, but they're not too easy. Pick this up if you can, definitely worth €10.

[u]Specs[/u]
Well, it's a game that's literally cmd with a pretty desktop. I'm pretty sure the oldest computer on Earth could run this.

NVIDIA GeForce GTX 750 Ti
8GB RAM

review_text_raw:
I'll say it straight, I am not a hacker or an expert programmer, although I had a minimal use of console clients and some programming basics, beside using consoles like DOS in my very first PCs. Hacknet is a hacking game entirely done through console commands and minimal interface in a fictional OS, you'll join tasks to do to go through a main story and a few side jobs, most of the game is all about typing codes on console, the faster you go the better you hack, there are just a few times you must stop and think how to proceed to get the informations or files you need, which is nothing impossible for a beginner. I liked this game for it's way to be different, not too difficult to learn, not too far from reality. 


[b][u]PROS[/u][/b]
[list]

[*][u]HACKING[/u]: There's not much space for hacking effects, beside a few simple animations, hacking goes all through a console, and that's the way real hackers work! The way it makes you feel is great, with some basic commands you can do anything you want without being an IT expert, actually teaching one thing or two about real hacking and consoles! I enjoyed this version of hacking better than unrealistic interactive ways from other games, thumbs up!

[*][u]DIFFICULTY[/u]: Difficulty is very balanced, at least for someone with my experience, it's all about learning a dozen commands, understand what they do and use them for your purposes, not too hard, neither too easy. Once you understand how to use them, you need to get faster and use logic to find what you need, which could be a hidden file or password, beginners shouldn't have too many problems, intermediates woul enjoy it, experts maybe would find it a bit too easy and boring.

[*][u]MINIMAL[/u]: Its minimal graphics just plays a good role, real hackers don't use animations and such, leaving it minimal gives it some realism and fashion, plus makes the game lighter. Thanks for leaving it as minimal as it would be in real hacking, with just very few add ons.

[*][u]STORY AND BACKSTORY[/u]: At first I had the feeling it was short and easy...and I was right, although the climax near the end was awesome, got me stuck into knowing the ending of it and hack into the very last hard tasks, I had to change my opinion about the story, it was good and interesting! There's a bit of backstory about the making of the game, explained by the developer himself, which makes the game's finale even better.

[*][u]WORKSHOP[/u]: I noticed the workshop is enabled and has extra missions and stories to download and play. I admit I didn't try anything from the workshop yet, but sounds like you can expand your game with some addons, which compensaty the main story's shortness and the game's price.

[*][u]SMOOTH AND LIGHT[/u]: Being mostly on console and so minimal, the game runs great on PC with very low hardware requirement. As far as the gameplay experience and fun are untouched, it's a good strong point to distribute the game to low end and PCs not made for gaming.


[/list]


[b][u]CONS[/u][/b]
[list]

[*][u]EYE BOILING[/u]: I've spent about 23 years in front of screens, starting from old CRTs, despite that I never had problems with my sight, either glasses or hurting eyes for long times. Despite that, Hacknet was the first and only game to give me eye pain, not fully sure if my sight is just failing or had a tiring day, but it never happened before. Watching the console for a few hours was a lot worse than I ever experienced before. So be careful, you may need some eye resting from time to time or just not play it for too long.

[*][u]END MISSION EMAILS[/u]: Just like real tasks, you don't win as soon as you reach your objective, most of times you need to send an email back to the contact and it will say if you completed your mission or not. Some tasks requires to write a password in the reply, that way you know what you need to find and what you need to write, but most of times it's all about sending a blank email back, if you didn't complete it, you'll get an error while trying to send the email. To cut it short, there are times you just need to access to files or servers and then answer the email, sometimes your objective is not so clear, so you will get stuck in the email before you fry your mind thinking about stuff you may have skipped or fry the game by reading a step-by-step guide, which kills the fun from the game. There were a few times that frustrated me, maybe giving more informations about the task or send back an email to give hints about the missing tasks would have been better.

[*][u]STORY LENGTH[/u]: Even if short and simple, I praised the story for its climax, but I can't hide a bit of disappointment for being so short, about 9-12 hours for the story, 3-4 extra hours to complete achievements and the other contracts and about 3-4 hours for the DLC (which I don't own nor tried). would have been perfect to almost double its time to make the game truly worth its price, but at least the workshop should help a bit more.

[/list]

Final word: Not too easy, not too hard, made for newbies curious about hacking and people with a bit of knowledge about it. If you accept the compromise to "play" on the console only, it will give you a true hacking feeling and about 10 hours of fun, and I loved it. Recommended for those people, especially if you can find it for a good price!

review_text_raw:
Lemme start by saying that this feels like it'd be a pretty niche title.  If the idea of entering commands into a terminal and making notes about IP addresses and passwords does not appeal to you, then turn away now since that's the majority of the gameplay here.


Hacknet fits into the very, very tiny genre of hacking games.  No, not Watch Dogs.  More like Uplink.  And... umm... others?  I honestly don't know of any other titles in this genre, to be honest!  It's a game about breaking into servers, looking for information, and then covering your tracks.  As the game progresses, you'll be tested on your ability to type accurately, multi-task quickly, and ability to dig deep for details in order to progress.  It's a satisfying experience, but I can see where this can get incredibly frustrating, or boring, for some.

Note:  I do not own the DLC and, therefore, it does not factor into this review.

The Good

-Somewhat simulates Real Life™ hacking, versus the "Hollywood" hacking used in Uplink.  It's cool, but I imagine its very simplied and toned down.  But, it's still really neat.

-Makes a fairly daunting premise pretty easy to figure out and play.  The tutorials explain things well enough and stuff isn't thrown at you too fast.  You won't get turned loose on your own until you have a firm grasp of things and you'll never get in over your head.

-Meanwhile, the game is still challenging enough you'll have to stop and think things through at times or get put into situations where the pressure is on and you can't afford to make mistakes.  

-Good music.  It's not great music, persay, but it sets the mood well and isn't distracting.  Not something I'd plan on listening to out of the game, but I definitely appreciate its presence.

-Workshop support is always a good thing to have in a game.  I've not tried the stuff out yet, but it seems like people can do things like add new missions and stuff, which is cool and can add a lot of longevity to the game.


The Neutral

-The plot...  its serviceable, but a bit predictable.  Kinda a shrug rating.


The Bad

-The cost might be one of them.  The game isn't very long and, combined with the next point, might make $10 a little steep.  Granted, there's incredibly few games in this sort of genre and mod support will help shore up the major short coming.

-The big, big, big point though, is the game is short and fairly linear and, therefore, has low replay value.  There's secrets to explore and discover and some parts of the game are procedurally generated, making for a somewhat different experience each time.  However, it lacks the open nature of Uplink, its progression systems, or two options of storylines.  Tools are given when you needed them, no sooner and no later.  Side unlock stuff are mostly cosmetic things, like new themes.  There's very few side missions and you'll have to do most of them to progress either way.  You're looking at 5-6 hours for a single play through and it'll feel like it's over just a little bit too soon.  This is no doubt the biggest thing to consider when thinking about buying this game.  Although, remember, Workshop support can potentially alleviate this issue.

-The server map gets rather unwieldly late game, as its hard to tell which server is which or select the right one.  Some sort of filtering tool would have been a huge help here, especially since most servers only get used once or twice and then never again.


All in all, this is a tough recommendation.  It's a fairly niche title and you may wish to wait for a sale to pick it up.  But there's very, very few experiences on the market that are anything like it, so it's definitely worth giving a shot if only for novelty's sake.

I've not tried the stuff out yet, but it seems like people can do things like add new missions and stuff, which is cool and can add a lot of longevity to the game. The Neutral -The plot... its serviceable, but a bit predictable. Kinda a shrug rating. The Bad -The cost might be one of them. The game isn't very long and, combined with the next point, might make $10 a little steep. Granted, there's incredibly few games in this sort of genre and mod support will help shore up the major short coming. -The big, big, big point though, is the game is short and fairly linear and, therefore, has low replay value. There's secrets to explore and discover and some parts of the game are procedurally generated, making for a somewhat different experience each time. However, it lacks the open nature of Uplink, its progression systems, or two options of storylines. Tools are given when you needed them, no sooner and no later. Side unlock stuff are mostly cosmetic things, like new themes. There's very few side missions and you'll have to do most of them to progress either way. You're looking at 5-6 hours for a single play through and it'll feel like it's over just a little bit too soon. This is no doubt the biggest thing to consider when thinking about buying this game. Although, remember, Workshop support can potentially alleviate this issue. -The server map gets rather unwieldly late game, as its hard to tell which server is which or select the right one. Some sort of filtering tool would have been a huge help here, especially since most servers only get used once or twice and then never again. All in all, this is a tough recommendation. It's a fairly niche title and you may wish to wait for a sale to pick it up. But there's very, very few experiences on the market that are anything like it, so it's definitely worth giving a shot if only for novelty's sake.

*Got the game for $2.99 during a sale*

Hacknet is an interesting game. Let's just get that out of the way. Its got a very good storyline and, while I have some experience in [strike]hacking[/strike] computer security, I didn't find (most) of the puzzles too difficult for the average person to solve. It sets a very good pace, picking up the difficulty very well. I'm writing this review just after completing the game, which took me just over 6 hours.

You start off with a message from Bit, telling you how to use the Hacknet software, etc. etc. Basically a tutorial on how to use it, the command line, that sort of thing. (If you're a linux user, this game will be much easier, the commands are basically the same for navigating the terminal and the like) After this, you're sent off to a hacker group, Entropy. You do a few hacks, and things start to pick up. You rise to the top (naturally) and start going off, investigating. I'd say more but I don't want to risk spoilers. The ending was very intriguing, and worth the effort.

The challenges are similar, but I never got bored of them. Find server at X IP, break down any proxies, firewalls, and open ports to use the almighty PortHack and get the admin password. Then, do whatever you need to, be it uploading or downloading a file, deleting stuff, or (later) even messing with databases and some... other devices. ([spoiler]a pacemaker[/spoiler]) They become more difficult as you progress, adding tracers that initiate an IP change failsafe if you take too long, more ports to open, and more complex firewalls and proxies. You'll need to grab passwords from emails and circumvent servers with powerful tracers, and even more interesting events. The only randomly difficult challenge that jumped me was an attack on my PC, which I was able to avoid using a [spoiler]trap shell[/spoiler]. If it gets you, there is a guide to help you out.

The interface is very intuitive and I never had any unreasonable issues with it, aside from becoming stuck when entering a password I didn't want to enter. (Which is my fault, I clicked login. What did I expect?) Later, you get the option to switch your layout, but none of them are really terrible. You have the terminal window (for commands), the display window (for showing the filesystem, passwords, databases, emails, etc.), the RAM window (watch this one, especially later when you get more RAM-hungry programs), and your NetMap (showing all the IPs you've connected to/can connect to).

The playtime was a good length. I would have liked it to be a bit longer but 6 hours is longer than AAA campaigns. God I hate AAA companies. Be innovative. Or I'll use Hacknet to take down your servers. /rant. Anyway, I'm not complaining about the length. As I said earlier, it never got repetitive, it was always interesting. There was always a sense of "oh gotta do this quickly or they're gonna catch me with that trace" that pushes you forward. Because of that speed though, don't play this game if you're not a quick typist. I have a speed of about 70 WPM (Faster now), which is well above average. I'd recommend being able to go above 40 WPM to play this effectively. 

------------------------------------------------------

Of course, what's a review without a pro/con list.

Pros:
+Good, interesting gameplay
+Active modding community (for extra levels and whatnot)
+Great value for the price (Yes, I know I got it for $2.99. But it's worth the full $9.99)
+Nice visuals (watch out, 1 looks like lowercase L. Tripped me up once)
+Easter Egg bash.org quotes
+Amazing soundtrack. Reflects the mood and urgency of the situations. 10/10 on that.

Neutrals:
+-Console window pops up behind game (Alt Tabbing is a little wierd)
+-Can't skip ending credits

Cons:
-You need to be a quick and accurate typist
-Requires some prior knowledge of terminal commands in order to be efficient (from the start)

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very interesting, non-repetitive gameplay and a good storyline. Visuals are of high quality and the soundtrack is amazing. However, to be good at this game you should be good at typing ( >40 WPM) and know how to navigate the Linux terminal, or at least pick up on it quickly. (I mean, it's just ls, cd, cat, and mv really) Also, bash.org quotes.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

I've just finished the Hacknet: Labyrinths DLC. I'm adding a short little note here about that.

Definetely worth it. Took an extra 3 and a half hours or so to complete, so pretty decent playtime. Much more interesing puzzles than the base game. You are tasked with completing the "Kaguya Trials" from the CSEC list, and join with a group of 3 other hackers. You'll take missions from a list and complete them with the help of the others. While you usually never actually interact with them other than seeing them in the IRC, it does feel like they're helping you. (I won't spoil how, but it becomes apparent in the endgame.) The challenges were a bit more difficult, but nothing that wasn't impossible. A mission towards the end just becomes a cat-and-mouse chase for a password, but while it didn't seem to guide you it wasn't that difficult to follow the clues. Overall, I'd highly rate the DLC. If you have the extra cash when buying Hacknet, I would recommend purchasing it. Do complete it after the main game though, or your NetMap will become a mess...

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very well done game and a great expansion to the original. I would definitely recommend purchasing this alongside the base game. Just... Play it after you beat the base game.

review_text_raw:
Super fun game. As someone who has basic knowledge into network/cybersecurity and has worked with UNIX terminals before it's immediately comfortable. I'm a bit of a slow learner but I found my rhythm relatively quickly. It does take a bit to get into the groove, I didn't find myself truly enjoying it until I was out of the tutorial and could choose my own missions and it felt more like a job than a learning obligation. Very interesting game design and it felt like more or less a perfect crossroads between simulating the complexity of the technology at hand (even though Naix was right- you're more or less just a script kiddie) and being a cool xD L33T H4XX0R game. 

Spoiler: [spoiler] My favorite mission was the pacemaker one. It gave you a background and a lead and basically said "alright, figure it out". It was a super surreal experience testing out a couple things to see if it would stop the heart and when my 3rd try actually worked I felt the real weight of a life on my hands. In contrast, the last lengthy mission with V to uncover Bit's past and everything was cool but it felt like I was getting handheld through the process and it was really annoying having to re-do some hacks (because I had missed some things and had to go back or wanted to double-check one of Bit's many servers) and suddenly encountering "unhackable" places. I didn't mind the slight shift to having to sleuth for passwords but it didn't come at the right time imo. [/spoiler]

A couple issues- the node map quickly gets crowded around the end of the game (and isn't really meaningfully sorted), meaning it gets a little annoying to find what you need. When you get to around the last couple missions when you have to visit a lot of nodes it gets kinda cumbersome. This is compounded by the fact that you sometimes have to re-hack nodes if you want to revisit them in case you missed something. Double backing to "double check" a machine already isn't a super pleasant feeling, so if you're digging through a cluster of nodes to find it, just to have to re-execute what could be a pretty lengthy hack just gets kind of frustrating. If there were better organization of nodes or an option to dim the brightness/opacity of nodes I don't really care about at the moment, it would be great. In addition, the graphics are a little messed up. De-selecting fullscreen makes the display expand greater than my monitor size (even though the game resolution matches my monitor resolution).

Otherwise- very fun game. Short length, about 5-8 hours to complete depending on your pace and experience on a terminal. Had a nice time spending my NYE on this one. Cheers!

review_text_raw:
Overview:
  Hacknet is at its heart a digital exploration game. Using a powerful suite of programs that you gain throughout the game, the player must gain access to systems and perform contracts. The game has a very similar feeling to the older game Uplink and hacking is done through speed, knowledge of your tools, and system resource management (RAM).

Plot:
  The plot is pretty threadbare, but does a good job of pulling the overarching story together. The ending makes sense, but is a little lacklustre for the scope of what you supposedly accomplish. However, this is in character for hacking since public attention is bad for those at the fringe of legality. Overall, I enjoyed the plot, but the beginning intro and ending are really the only interesting points. It's difficult to do characterization when all you have is text, but I felt that more effort could have been put into letting the player get to know more of the other people in the story (naix, maybe some backstory on bit, etc.)
 
Gameplay:
  The gameplay is separated into two parts: hacking and forensics. The actual hacking is rather easy since most trace timers last far more than long enough and some systems actually keep your admin after you disconnect. The main challenge in this format is simply knowing which order to run the port hacking programs in so that you can maximize efficiency and minimize time spent not logged in. These do get quite intense at times and a few conflict sequences definitely run the point home that you're not invulnerable. Progress through the game is blocked in a sort of metroid-vania way, in the sense that you need this power to unlock that type of port to enter. I enjoyed this, but wished that there were more early systems that you needed to backtrack to.

  That backtracking is part of the second part of the gameplay, the forensics. By this I mean that you spend your time going through file systems trying to spot the file with the password, scanning computers to reach connected nodes, and searching for new IPs to check out. In fact, there is an entirely alternative gameplay path that is only reached with diligent use of your tools. I loved the exploring, but it did feel quite limited, or at the very least truncated to be more accessable for players who might not be used to the gameplay style.
  Part of the joy of the exploration comes from the humor that you find in random files. From a script for "Titanic 2" that involves the icebergs running onto land and attacking people to Bash.org IRC logs, there is a decent amount of silliness and joy to discover. However, since the files in the systems you hack are procedurally generated, more content would have been nice. There's only so many times that you can see the same Bash log before you stop wanting 
to check them out because you feel you've seen everything.

Pros:
*really fun
*sense of satisfaction from difficult hacks
*humor: From a mission where you need to write "d*cks" on the main webpage of "Nortron Security" to an homage to *chans (the secret /el/ image board), the game is very funny and self aware.
*exploration
*failure penalty fair
*short: Hacknet doesn't wear out its welcome, which it probably would have for some players by the end game.

Cons:
*repetitive
*short
*not enough content
*exploration feels like it was stunted for ease of access

Hopes:
*mods:
	I feel that mods could make this from a good game to a great game. I'd love to try my hand at adding new features to the game.
*hardware changes
	Uplink let the player purchase hardware upgrades to increase ram or processing power as well as giving access to more complicated systems. Hacknet's only customization for your computer is changing the display theme.
*more story
	Getting to know the other hackers more personally would be very enjoyable.
*higher difficulty
	clearing the logs on a system means that they won't track you down - but this presents a problem. You always leave a disconnect log, but the game doesn't notice that a disconnect log without a matching connect log implies
	that the IP that disconnected was responsible for the attack. Having to selectively clear logs and/or bounce IP like Uplink might be a good idea. In addition, I would have enjoyed more difficult forensics and encrypted files
	that you can't find the password for. I was a little miffed a few times when I spent some time looking through the files to find the next IP when all I had to do was type "scan". More threats to the player as well as uncertainty
	in how well you performed the attack would be welcome.
*more challenges
	Maybe adding in new network architecture requiring the player to do a different minigame than typing the first two letters of a program and tab completing.
*multiplayer
	multiplayer is hinted at being in development in the files on the endgame server.

Bottom Line:
I love this game and want to spend so much more time on it, but sadly it seems that there's no more content. This type of game is sadly lacking in today's market and is quite unique. It pulls off what it does well and with much better guidance than Uplink. You should try it if you're interested in learning basic cmd/*nix commands and command line navigation/use while having fun, if you like tech and silly games, or if you're a fan of Uplink.

review_text_raw:
A short but sweet game that may be especially interesting for people new to the command line / terminal interface. While the 'hacking' is somewhat shallow, the story is interesting. Intense time-pressure situations force you to apply your new knowledge, and fast; you must find, copy, delete, modify, scan, etc. before you're traced. It feels great to build up new hacking programs; Hacknet reveals its secrets at a natural pace.

The early missions are basic, to help you warm up your execution speed. When missions become complex (breadcrumb trails from one computer to the next), take unexpected turns, or introduce surprising new concepts and goals, Hacknet becomes truly excellent. It is not a stretch to say that the entire purpose of Hacknet is to prepare you for three or four outstanding missions - if the regular missions are engaging, these special ones inspire everything from terror to intense focus: they strain your hacking speed, your memory as you piece together a puzzle of scattered info, and inspire that conspiratorial feeling of getting closer to the hidden truth.

Hacknet doesn't outstay its welcome - it ends when all the available mechanics have been thoroughly explored and challenged, and no later. The campaign can be cleared in about six hours, and the remaining secrets and alternate paths can be tackled in another three hours (postgame knowledge and skills allow you to blast through the early missions in minutes, on subsequent playthroughs - this also feels great). 

Though its short length and limited replayability keep Hacknet out of 'classic territory', I would recommend it as a fun, fast way to get familiar with the basic concepts of terminal navigation and file editing(!). [Note: I was familiar with terminals before playing]

Hints for new players: 
1.) Don't forget about 'ps' and 'kill', they may save your life.

2.) If you find yourself in contact with a new faction or individual you want to follow-up with, do not complete or initiate missions with any other factions. [i]Completing one faction's mission while multiple paths are available will lock you into that faction's path[/i], closing off the others. [spoiler]You'll eventually end up in CSEC, no matter what[/spoiler]

3.) Use addNote for the tough stuff, but try to use your own memory whenever you can. It never hurts to download a file so you have a password on record.

4.) When in doubt, 'dc'.

What a great game. I acquired this in a Humble Bundle recently with a few other titles. Hacknet, for lack of better words, is a Unix-based hacking simulator in which you use the combination of a point-and-click interface and a command prompt to explore the mysterious death of a hacker named "Bit." Bit has arranged to send automated messages to you posthumously, giving you leads that are just enough for you to find your way.

Being not much of a programmer, and unfamiliar with Linux and Unix-based command systems (idk man I just look stuff up and punch shit into the Windows 10 command prompt and sometimes it says words back to me), I felt learning to play Hacknet might be too daunting of a task. However, the feeling subsided in less than half an hour, when I was able to navigate through any device's file systems with ease, hopping from device to device, opening ports, cracking passwords, etc. Not long after that was I very immersed in the story (something I have a hard time being in MANY games).

While some aspects of the game can be done through clicking between devices, folders, and apps, other things are seemingly only possible by using the command-line, keeping the game immersive and making you feel, in a sense, accomplished. YOU cracked open all of Macrosoft's ports and got to snoop around in their sensitive files. YOU found a security loophole by exploiting a computer's connected smartphone. YOU made a clean getaway just in time before having your IP traced, clearing the system logs and running for the hills with some juicy new program you can use to hack *even more* devices. And you did it all with your analytical skills and an intuitive command system. In fact, there's even a point in the game where your OS/interface is essentially deleted from your system by another angry hacker, leaving you with a big black command terminal, having to plot through your own computer to restore the deleted files and get yourself back in the game. Just like in real life, each device you access seems like a sum of its parts, even your own.

The IP tracing mechanic is excellent, and pretty much exactly what you'd imagine seeing on some Hollywood hacker's monitor. It keeps the pressure on, even if it is slow at times. RAM management, learning what ports to use when, and being able to type quickly and remember which programs do what are important, and make hacking into each and every system rewarding in its own way, even if it doesn't have quite what you were looking for.

The visual effects are excellent, if a bit cheesy at times. The interface is simple enough that these "glitchy" or "tech-y" effects aren't too jarring unless they need to be, which keeps the game immersive but also fun to watch. I'd advise that anyone with epilepsy be careful with this game at some times - lots of effects are fast or flashy in nature.

The story doesn't seem to thrust itself into your face at all. Save for the occasional automated (but justified) email from Bit, you discover all of the story on your own, and every lead and new piece of information feels genuine and is worth discovering.

Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game. Two complaints (which end up not really being complaints after I explain them):

- The IP map, showing all known devices and their IPs, can get a bit cluttered, and it's easy to forget where one particular computer is on the big web of spinning circles and lines connecting them. The position of an IP address on the map is not always intuitive. However, this could arguably help with immersion, making you feel like you're navigating through a web of IP addresses. It's the internet in its raw form - not catered to your viewing pleasure.

- I'm left wanting more. Not that I didn't get my money's worth, but I want more. But that's something every game should strive for - leaving you wanting more, and not outstaying its welcome.

Challenging, but *very* rewarding command system that makes you feel clever. Decent story that keeps you invested throughout the game. Findable humorous IRC logs, detailing early Internet culture, which I think are ripped straight from Bash.org, meaning they are real logs written by real people. Stereotypical electronic "hacker" soundtrack which helps the atmosphere of the game.

If any of this interests you, definitely get Hacknet, especially if it's in a bundle or on sale.

Story 8/10
I found the story very intriguing and it grabbed me right away, I almost finished the game in one sessions because I was that engrossed with how it was turning out. I really do wish this game was more fleshed out in the way that you could go either white hat, gray hat, or black hat. Different routes would be absolutely AMAZING, but it doesn't take away from the game at all and it's 100% worth the price. Would love to enjoy more content from the creators.

The interface was simple yet during the more hectic missions it's complex enough that multitasking demanded my full attention in order to keep up. Again, I had a metric shit ton of fun with this game. I would recommend that if you get stuck to think things through without gunning for a guide on the internet. I also would have loved to have been able to upgrade my hardware and software, but for a short game it's not needed at all (I think I finished the game in approx. 7 hours or so, I felt like I was really going through it kinda fast, but then again I do have knowledge in this field and I don't recall getting stuck for any long period of time.) I can't stress enough how much fun I had, I started this game around midnight and didn't even realize just how engrossed I was until I looked outside to see the sun had already risen.

If you're in any way interested in the security field, I HIGHLY recommend picking this up. It was a blast to play and the price can't be beat. 5/7 would accidentally delete everyone's degrees again (OOPS :P)

100% worth

Hacknet is not "an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator for PC", this here is just a lie and I actually would say may be a detriment to the game depending on who you are and how you take those words.

If you're like me and you essentially expected a hacking simulator where you did as you please, hacked who you wanted to hack, and cause mayhem or the like, this is not what this game is about. You're better off looking at Uplink and getting UplinkOS.

What you're really getting from Hacknet is actually a sort of immersive novel, but you're a silent protagonist who probably button mashes the keyboard when sending e-mails.

Hacknet is very much the story about a recently deceased hacker named Bit. It's very much about trying to uncover what it was that Bit was doing that got him killed.

Hacknet is not a game you are going to be spending nearly 20 hours of your life playing though. At the moment of writing, I have 17, but that mostly comes from me picking the game back up again in previous attempts to play the game, and realizing that I have no idea what I'm doing at all, and starting back from the beginning to figure out what things did what.

The reality is, this game is actually about 8 hours or so in length, maybe a couple more if you get a tad lost. It's sort of hard to say, I would also wager it could be 10.

[b]But a thumbs up though, why?[/b] Well that's simply because this game does something interesting in all of this, and that is create interesting setups here and there for you to complete. Be it in one instance hacking into a fictional fast food chicken restaurants servers to find their secret recipe, death row records, [i]hospital equipment[/i], or deleting the save file of a user from a clicker game, Hacknet tries to give you interesting jobs in what would become a tedious routine for some.

If you're looking for a simulation where you are a hacker paid by big companies to take on big jobs against individuals and other companies, look to Uplink for that, especially with the UplinkOS GUI mod.

And then this is where I tell you "but if you're looking for...", cause it's hard to pin Hacknet's strength. Like I said, it has good setups for its missions, but the actual main plot is honestly kind of weak. So why do I still recommend it? I guess it's in the charm of it all quite frankly between the music, the flashy aesthetic, and all that.

Like honestly, the ONLY reason I actually finally got through the main plot of this game was because a video got recommended to me of the games last mission out of context, and everything on screen along with Carpenter Brut's "Roller Mobster" was enough to make me think "What's going on?" and play though the game just to see what was up. And honestly it was a bit underwhelming once it was all said and done, lol

So do I still recommend this game?

It's 10USD, and it often goes on sale for like less than 2USD, so I'd either way.

Is the DLC worth it? I actually think the last mission of the DLC is better as it gives a far better "emotion" to you the player as you're doing it, so totally consider picking it up if it's on sale.

Also it's absolute bullcrap I can't do "rm -rf /" or any such variation of such. I don't care if teaching newbs the most dangerous command might make them also do it to their own terminal on accident, that's their fault and mine if I'm not paying attention.

Seriously, it would have made the last mission just more hilarious to just do that, crack open a can of coke, and just watch and wait for everything to delete.

Hacknet is an absolute gem of a game. 

[b]TLDR: [/b]While people already familiar with using *nix or general programing principles may find this game not too deep or challenging, it offers a well thought out narrative, with fun game mechanics and excels at teaching you about computer essentials without you even realizing it. 


[b]More thoughts:[/b] 

While this game isn't perfect, I would still reccomend it to anyone who has even a remote interest in computers. Even if you only want to feel like a hacker in a movie, that game gives you that feeling. If you want to learn more about the general concepts of computer-, program-, and network-architecture, this game is a great launching-point, before you start reading more "serious" or conventional literature on the subject. 

Now, the mechanics are pretty straight-forward. You gain various programs through completing quests, which, in turn, can be used to bypass more complex security. You also gain the ability to run commands through other computers, allowing you, for example, to pretty much emulate a DDOS attack. Timing is also important, so be ready to type "dc" + [enter] if you're being tracked. AAAAAAAAANNNNNNDDDDDD............

.....
.....
.....

that's pretty much it when it comes to mechanics. The rest is working your way through systems full of mostly text-files, a lot of them taken from bash.org (hilarious quotes from internet chats, NSFW, but great!), and a lot of fun easter-eggs for nerds and fans of "hacker-culture" as it has been created by Hollywood. There even are multiple references to the movie "Hackers", a must see in my opinion. ;)

Now, the mechanics got old after not too long (a good 8 hours), mainly due to you unlocking a lot of the tools that you need pretty quickly. I'll talk more about overall gameplay features in just a moment. 

The narrative is fun, well paced, and interwoven well with the gameplay mechanics. I won't spoil anything, just watch the trailer and you get the general premise. 

The overall game is simplified, to allow people without prior experience to enjoy it, but encourages experimentation and exploration of what you can do, giving you plenty of examples and hints along the way to teach you, without you even realizing it, a lot about how your system works. Absolutely amazing!

Concerning the lack of gameplay features, the dev is amazing. Yup, one dev. And he's already said that he wants to implement multiplayer. If that happens, this will become one of the best games out there. Period. Plus he wants to continue to push content for the game. Not to mention, that the community as a whole is awesome and really suportive for newcomers. 

In its current state, it's well worth the price its asking for. As the dev continues to push more content, the game will continue to expand and improve. 

Please support this game, as its honestly trying to be different and fun, without a lot of the backstabbing and abusive tactics emplyed by all too many triple AAA studios/publishers. I can guarantee, you'll have a blast playing this!

Edit 2016: what I've said before still applies. I would just like to point towards the roadmap the dev has for 2016, which includes multiplayer and steam-workshop integration for custom missions throughout various points this year. http://steamcommunity.com/games/365450/announcements/detail/955130645658936382 

****DISCLAIMER:****
 WIll not actually refund any purchases if you are somehow not pleased with the overall game. 
Mouse and Mechanical Keyboard sold seperatly.
Batteries not included.

***This only takes the base game into account***

Ever wanted to crack down on some real terminal action to get a peek at what this hacking business is all about? Wonder no more, as Hacknet is here to "teach" you what "hacking" is. 

Immersive, intelligent and just enough unix-commands at your disposal, Hacknet will convince anyone not computer savvy or not paying close enough attention that the things on your monitor sure looks like something you shouldn't be doing, almost like dark wizardry magic. For the most part, the game offers up this illusion at an convincing rate while being beginner-friendly. However, in the world of hacking, there is very little hand holding, so the faster you understand what the ropes are, the better.

To deliver a convincing hacking experience, music is paramount - as Uplink back in the day taught everyone. Here is really delivers, with everything from ambient barrens tunes fit for the breaks between each mission, to serious business from The Algorithm and wildly intense adrenaline pumping Carpenter Brut songs. Hats off, this album is even worth listening to way after you've finished the game. 

As for the the main story, while not top shelf, is interesting enough to keep searching around for clues and getting a better grasp at what's going. As with any self respecting game that depicts hacking, it should have its sheer selectino of surprise elements, and Hacknet doesn't disappoint. However, this is usually found in side missions. The main story should've done more of that as well.

For each time you play, the game changes up names, IPs etc for the nodes to try to keep things sort of fresh, but the missions are mostly the same. All in all, Hacknet is a very solid, albeit simple at times, attempt at creating an immersive, "real enough" hacking simulator that most importantly is -FUN-. The list of unix commands are however at times frustratingly limited, especially if you know what you're doing. Since most of the game is very well laid out in terms of the interface, you start taking it for granted that you should be able to do more than you actually are allowed to. 

For example, "rm file*" will not work since the terminal doesn't support wildcards. Pathing is also needlessly tedious, as it doesn't properly understand using root-nodes in paths. Props however for making it possible to furk up yourself, which is how it should be. Paying attention and going "outside the beaten path" is usually rewarded.
 
Hacknet requires reading and understanding of its core concepts to get the most out of the experience. For those persistent enough, the game also delivers some hilarious content as a nod to the efforts. Here's to hoping the developer makes more content to this game, as the main game is rather short. It'll take you only around 5-6 hours for the main campaign. A multiplayer mode would've been awesome in addition to random missions. 

Rating: 8/10 - Play it!

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a hacking simulation in the vein of Introversion's fantastic Uplink. It provides the player a virtual OS from which to interact with 'nodes' dotted around the map. Each node represents a computer system which can be approached using the software and hardware knowledge you accumulate throughout the game. Pretty simple stuff on the surface, but Hacknet is a fantastically well-designed story-driven experience, with considerable replay value which will only continue to grow as new content is invariably released.

This game deserves praise for it's graphics, in that they perfectly fit the tone of the game. In most other game genres we typically see a push toward more cutting-edge photo-realism, but here we have a clean, crisp environment that doesn't over-burden or confuse the player with menus and tedious repetitive interaction. Praise is also due to the sound design in this title. The music is, again, a perfect fit for the game's tone. Orchesteral strings move to thumping bass adding a sense of pressure and drive that has kept me going back just for the music.


There are some problems with this game however. Some people will say these aren't problems as such, more personal gripes, but take them however you wish. 

1. It's short. Like really short. With no experience whatsoever, my first run was just under 3 hours from start to finish, completing every avaliable mission in the game aside from 'Junebug' which was bugged at the time. Hopefully, more content will be added soon, and the ability to open story creation to the community is an exciting prospect shound it be considered.

2. It's easy. The learning curve is pretty shallow, with a few basic commands covering every action you will be performing. Once you have got launching cracks using the TAB key down to a fine art, you can smash through any security in next to no time.

3. No Upgrade abilities. A key component of every computer interface is the hardware it's connected to, and in a game setting the ability to upgrade and customise that hardware is a given. There is no such system here. The only resource you have is RAM, which is set throughout the game and cannot be improved upon. This does give the game a streamlined feel, but I would still rather have an functioning economy and avenues to explore with my earnings.

Overall, I think Hacknet deserves your time if you enjoy the genre. If you do enjoy this quite esoteric game style, then you've no doubt played the alternatives. On balance, I would say that Onlink, the fan-made re-write of Uplink is the superior game in this category still. It is a longer, more challenging experience. That being said, with expansion and dedication, Hacknet will become the standard by which all other hacking simulation games will be judged. We should all help it get there, and enjoy the rewards when they come.

Buy it.
